## Description

The Lin-Bairstow method finds the roots of a real polynomial $P(x) = a_n x^n + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0$ two at a time, by finding a quadratic factor $x^2 - rx - s$.
It uses only real arithmetic, yet finds complex-conjugate pairs of roots as well as real ones.

Dividing $P(x)$ by $x^2 - rx - s$ leaves a quotient $Q(x)$ and a remainder,

$$
P(x) = (x^2 - rx - s)\,Q(x) + b_1 (x - r) + b_0, \qquad Q(x) = b_n x^{n-2} + \cdots + b_3 x + b_2 ,
$$

where quadratic synthetic division computes the $b$'s, and the same recursion applied to the $b$'s gives the $c$'s:

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_n &= a_n, & b_{n-1} &= a_{n-1} + r\,b_n, & b_k &= a_k + r\,b_{k+1} + s\,b_{k+2} \quad (k = n-2, \ldots, 1, 0), \\
c_n &= b_n, & c_{n-1} &= b_{n-1} + r\,c_n, & c_k &= b_k + r\,c_{k+1} + s\,c_{k+2} \quad (k = n-2, \ldots, 2, 1).
\end{aligned}
$$

The quadratic is a factor exactly when $b_0 = b_1 = 0$, and the method is Newton's method on these two equations in $r$ and $s$.
The $c$'s are the partial derivatives ($\partial b_0/\partial r = c_1$, $\partial b_0/\partial s = \partial b_1/\partial r = c_2$, $\partial b_1/\partial s = c_3$), so each step evaluates them at $(r_j, s_j)$ and solves, by Cramer's rule in Mathews' module,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} c_1 & c_2 \\ c_2 & c_3 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \Delta r \\ \Delta s \end{pmatrix}
= -\begin{pmatrix} b_0 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad r_{j+1} = r_j + \Delta r, \quad s_{j+1} = s_j + \Delta s .
$$

The method needs degree $n \ge 3$, a starting guess $(r_0, s_0)$, and $c_1 c_3 - c_2^2 \neq 0$ at every iterate.
Real starts keep the iterates real, and a real polynomial always has a real quadratic factor.
Mathews suggests $r_0 = -a_1/a_2$, $s_0 = -a_0/a_2$ (if $a_2 \neq 0$), from $P(x) \approx a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$ near $x = 0$.

In general, Newton's method for a smooth system converges quadratically from close enough starts when its Jacobian is nonsingular at the solution.
Here that holds exactly when $x^2 - rx - s$ and $Q(x)$ have no common root, as when every root of $P$ is simple.
When they share one, convergence can drop to linear: for $P(x) = (x^2 + 1)^2$ from $(0.1, -1.2)$, the error ratio tends to $1/2$.

For Mathews' Example 4 ([Case 1](#case-1)), $P(x) = x^4 + x^3 + 3x^2 + 4x + 6$ from $(r_0, s_0) = (-2.1, -1.9)$, the iterates converge to $x^2 + 2x + 2$, with roots $-1 \pm i$, and $Q(x) = x^2 - x + 3$ gives $\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{11}}{2} i$.
From step 2 on, the error's exponent roughly doubles each step (errors from 40-digit arithmetic):

| $j$ | $r_j$ | $s_j$ | error $\lVert (r_j + 2,\, s_j + 2) \rVert$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | −2.1 | −1.9 | $1.41 \times 10^{-1}$ |
| 1 | −1.989302820836 | −1.949988192338 | $5.11 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| 2 | −1.999992769905 | −2.000150979221 | $1.51 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | −1.999999996545 | −1.999999991124 | $9.52 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| 4 | −2.000000000000 | −2.000000000000 | $1.42 \times 10^{-17}$ |

Repeating the method on $Q(x)$ (deflation, [Case 2](#case-2)) finds the rest.
For the quintic $x^5 + 6x^4 - 20x^2 + 22x + 8$ of Mathews' Examples 1–3, the start $(-2, 3)$, his divisor $x^2 + 2x - 3$, gives $x^2 + 3.238964x + 0.853460$ (roots $-2.949618$, $-0.289346$); his suggested start on the cubic quotient gives $x^2 - 2.301046x + 1.851731$ (roots $1.150523 \pm 0.726655i$), leaving $x + 5.062082$.

Convergence is only local.
From $(r_0, s_0) = (-1, -2)$ on the same quintic, the iterates are thrown out to $|s_{26}| \approx 7 \times 10^8$ and wander for more than 90 steps, and the factor they reach depends on the arithmetic: $x^2 - 2.301046x + 1.851731$ in double precision, $x^2 + 8.011701x + 14.931211$ with 30 or more digits.

Quadratic synthetic division extends the division by $x - c$ of [Horner's Method](../horners-method.qmd), the iteration is two-variable [Newton-Raphson](../newton-raphson-method/) as in [Nonlinear Systems](../nonlinear-systems/), [Graeffe's Method](../graeffes-method/) is another method made for polynomials, and [Muller's Method](../mullers-method/) can also reach complex roots, using complex arithmetic.

## Animations

Mathews made no animation for the Lin-Bairstow method, so both animations below are new, with no Mathews original.
Most frames show one Lin-Bairstow step; Case 2 also has a frame for each deflation.
In the complex-plane panels, red dots are the two roots of the current trial factor $x^2 - r_j x - s_j$; the method works only with the real numbers $r_j$ and $s_j$, and the roots are drawn (by the quadratic formula) only to show where the factor is heading.
Open circles mark the roots of $P$.
Case 1 follows a single factor closely, zooming in as the steps shrink; Case 2 repeats the method on the quotients until every root of a quintic is found.
Mathews' Examples 1–3, which divide the quintic once by $x^2 + 2x - 3$ (by formula, by tableau and in vector form), are not animated as such, since each is one division rather than an iteration; they are step 0 of Case 2.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

### Case 1 — Mathews' Example 4, $P(x) = x^4 + x^3 + 3x^2 + 4x + 6$, $(r_0, s_0) = (-2.1, -1.9)$ {#case-1}

**Behavior:** The iterates converge to $(r, s) = (-2, -2)$, the factor $x^2 + 2x + 2$, whose roots $-1 \pm i$ are a complex pair although every iterate is real.
The top-left panel shows $(r_j + 2,\, s_j + 2)$, zoomed in each frame so that the previous iterate (open circle) and the current one (red) both fit; the window shrinks from $\pm 0.13$ at step 0 to $\pm 1.7 \times 10^{-17}$ at step 5.
The top-right panel shows the trial roots at full scale: they start at $-1.05 \pm 0.893i$ and are already within 0.021 of $-1 \pm i$ at step 1, too close to see at this scale, so the bottom-left panel zooms in on the upper root $x_+$ in the same way; its distance from $-1 + i$ falls through $0.118$, $0.0206$, $7.92 \times 10^{-5}$, $3.21 \times 10^{-9}$, $4.72 \times 10^{-18}$, $1.04 \times 10^{-35}$.
The bottom-right panel plots $\log_{10}$ of the error $\lVert (r_j + 2,\, s_j + 2) \rVert$: after a slow first step ($0.141$ to $0.0511$), its exponent roughly doubles each step from $j = 2$ on ($-3.8$, $-8.0$, $-16.8$, $-34.5$), the mark of quadratic convergence.
The iterates are those of the table above and agree with the ones Mathews prints to at least 14 decimal places; the script runs in 256-bit arithmetic so that steps 4 and 5, whose errors are far below double-precision round-off, show the method's own error (in double precision, $r_4 = s_4 = -2$ exactly).
The gray circles are the roots $\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{11}}{2} i \approx 0.5 \pm 1.658i$ of the other factor, $Q(x) = x^2 - x + 3$.

[Julia source](bairstowaa.jl)

![Lin-Bairstow animation for P(x) = x⁴ + x³ + 3x² + 4x + 6 from (r₀, s₀) = (−2.1, −1.9), five steps in four panels: the (r, s) iterates approaching (−2, −2) in a window that zooms in each frame; the two roots of x² − r x − s moving onto −1 ± i in the complex plane, with the roots 0.5 ± 1.658i of the other factor shown in gray; a zoom on the upper root approaching −1 + i; and the base-10 logarithm of the error, which falls from 1.41e−01 to 3.19e−35 with its exponent roughly doubling each step from step 2](bairstowaa.gif)

### Case 2 — Deflation, $P(x) = x^5 + 6x^4 - 20x^2 + 22x + 8$ {#case-2}

**Behavior:** Stage 1 starts from Mathews' divisor $x^2 + 2x - 3$, $(r_0, s_0) = (-2, 3)$; step 0 is his Example 1, with remainder $3(x + 2) + 8$, so $b_1 = 3$ and $b_0 = 8$.
The trial roots, 1 and $-3$ at the start, stay real and converge to $-0.289346$ and $-2.949618$; each stage stops at the first step with $|\Delta r| + |\Delta s| < 10^{-12}$, here step 6, and the line under the plot shows the remainder $b_0$ falling from 8 to about $10^{-14}$, the level of double-precision round-off.
Deflation leaves the cubic $x^3 + 2.761036x^2 - 9.796356x + 9.373612$, and stage 2 starts from Mathews' suggestion for it, $r_0 = -a_1/a_2 = 3.548073$, $s_0 = -a_0/a_2 = -3.394962$.
Its trial roots start as the complex pair $1.774 \pm 0.498i$, become the real pair $2.146$ and $0.160$ at step 1, and are a complex pair again from step 2 on, converging to $1.150523 \pm 0.726655i$ (the stage stops at step 5).
The iterates $r_j, s_j$ are real throughout; the sign of $r_j^2 + 4s_j$ ($-0.99$, $3.94$, $-2.10$ at steps 0, 1, 2) decides whether the trial roots are real or complex.
The linear quotient $x + 5.062082$ gives the fifth root, $-5.062082$.
From step 2 on in each stage the trial roots sit on their circles at this scale, and only the remainder line shows the rest of the convergence.
The open circles are the eigenvalues of $P$'s companion matrix, computed independently of the deflation; the five roots found agree with them within $3.6 \times 10^{-15}$, and against roots computed with 60 digits the eigenvalues are off by up to $3.5 \times 10^{-15}$ and the deflation roots by at most $2.2 \times 10^{-16}$.

[Julia source](bairstowbb.jl)
